clue.text: Specially illuminated set of old books torn on the outside

indicators.note: The tear is placed round the edge of the other piece, so one word wraps the other instead of standing next to it.

parts.note: something torn has been split
OT is the Old Testament, the older half of the Bible and so a set of old books

explanation.walkthrough: OT is worth banking: any 'old books', 'old writings' or 'part of scripture' in a clue is nearly always those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Specially illuminated -> SPOTLIT: picked out by a spotlight, the beam that singles one figure out of a stage left otherwise dark.

clue.text: Bird, one on lake after daily drink?

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing sitting on another is written above it, so the letter for the number goes in first and the water below it.
Coming after something means being written behind it, so the drink is laid down first and the rest trails along at the end.

parts.note: a pinta is a pint of milk, from the doorstep advertising slogan
the Roman numeral for one
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinka pinta milka day' put PINTA into English and it lives nowhere else, which is exactly why the clue has to say daily.
explanation.definitionFit: Bird -> PINTAIL: a wild duck named for the drake's long pointed tail feathers, so the general word is pointing at one species.

clue.text: The royal I found in upsetting fate — it's absorbing?

definitions.note: The setter defines the thing by what it does rather than naming it: 'it' stands for the answer, so a clause takes the place of a noun.

indicators.note: Something upset is tipped over, and in a down entry that means its letters are read from the bottom upwards.
To be found in something is to sit inside it, so the two letters go between the others rather than beside them.

parts.note: your lot is your fate, what falls to you
a monarch says 'we' where the rest of us say 'I' — the royal we

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the join: everything before it builds the word, and the comment after it is the definition dressed up as a remark about the story.
explanation.definitionFit: it’s absorbing -> TOWEL: soaking up water is the whole job of one, so the clue names it by the property instead of the object.

clue.text: One bit of nut is stuck in my tooth

indicators.note: Anything stuck in a place is wedged within it, so those letters interrupt the word rather than following it.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: Ask for a bit of something and you break a piece off the front, so only the opening letter of the word is used.

parts.note: the front letter of nut
'cor!' and 'my!' are the same exclamation of surprise
the clue's own word, taken as it stands

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dental emergency and the step that unlocks it is hearing 'my' as an exclamation rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: tooth -> INCISOR: the flat chisel-shaped cutters at the front of the mouth, so the definition names the class and the answer one kind of it.

clue.text: Wine that's drunk always cold makes a pile for the country dweller

definitions.text: a pile for the country dweller

indicators.note: Wine that is drunk has been taken inside, so this wine swallows the letters that come after it instead of standing beside them.

parts.note: hock is the Rhine white, the crossword's usual wine
ay is the poets' word for ever and always, as in 'for ay'
C is cold, the letter on a tap

explanation.walkthrough: Two old conventions in one short clue, and the surface hides both by talking about a chilled glass of white.
explanation.definitionFit: a pile for the country dweller -> HAYCOCK: the cone-shaped heap a farmer forks hay into out in the field before it is carted in.

clue.text: A bishop must get by, having welcomed a Catholic in ecclesiastical office

indicators.note: To welcome guests is to have them in the house, so what is welcomed lands inside the word rather than after it.

parts.note: the clue's own opening letter, taken as it stands
B is the bishop on a chess scoresheet
the preposition taken whole, as two letters
the article, taken as a letter again
C is the standard shortening of Catholic, as in RC

explanation.walkthrough: Everything here is an abbreviation, which is why the pious surface runs so smoothly — nothing in it has to mean anything at all.
explanation.definitionFit: ecclesiastical office -> ABBACY: the position an abbot holds, the office itself rather than the man who holds it or the monastery he runs.

clue.text: Conservative minister entertaining those from the ranks — someone putting the record straight?

indicators.note: Entertaining people means having them inside your house, so the guests go between the other letters rather than alongside.

parts.note: C is Conservative on a ballot paper
OR is other ranks, the army's name for everyone who is not an officer
a rector is a parish minister

explanation.walkthrough: OR for other ranks earns its keep here: any clue mentioning soldiers, men or the ranks is usually asking for those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: someone putting the record straight -> CORRECTOR: the printing trade's corrector reads proofs and marks the errors, so the phrase names the job by what it does.

clue.text: Like tree worse affected by fungus — one penetrating horse chestnut

definitions.text: Like tree worse affected by fungus

indicators.note: To penetrate something is to go right into it, so the single letter is driven inside the word rather than added on the end.

parts.note: a conker is the seed of the horse chestnut
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: The clue turns on two lives of one word: the conker children play with, and 'conk', the shelf fungus a rotting trunk puts out.
explanation.definitionFit: Like tree worse affected by fungus -> CONKIER: conk is the bracket fungus growing on a trunk, so the comparative means more of it.

clue.text: The old way engineer catches fish with something wooden

indicators.note: A catch closes around whatever it holds, so the engineer's name opens up and the rest of the wordplay is trapped inside it.

parts.note: James Watt is the crossword's default engineer
the ling is a long cod-like sea fish
a tree is the wooden thing par excellence

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the road's second word is never clued as a road at all — it arrives as a tree, inside the engineer's own name.
explanation.definitionFit: The old way -> WATLING STREET: the Roman road running from Dover through London to Wroxeter, a way in the ancient sense of a made highway.

clue.text: Coke spells out end of dryness for the moment

indicators.note: What comes at the end of a word is its final letter, so only the closing one of the long word is taken.

parts.note: the letter this word finishes on
for the moment is for now

explanation.walkthrough: 'For the moment' is worth banking: at present, just now and for now all buy the same three letters in this game.
explanation.definitionFit: Coke -> SNOW: both are street names for cocaine, snow after the white powder it is sold as, so the definition is slang for slang.

clue.text: Moving awkwardly using clutch when straddling warning sign

indicators.note: To straddle something is to stand with a leg either side of it, so the word doing it ends up wrapped round the other.

parts.note: to clutch at something is to cling to it
amber is the middle traffic light, the warning that a stop is coming

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' is a verb here, not the pedal the driving surface is steering you towards, and that is the whole misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving awkwardly -> CLAMBERING: climbing on hands and knees over something difficult, which is exactly the graceless scramble described.

clue.text: Old rustics admitting love for pretender Don

indicators.note: A club that admits someone lets them through the door, so the letter goes inside the word rather than after it.

parts.note: a carl is an old word for a countryman or churl
love is nothing in tennis, and nothing is O

explanation.walkthrough: Love has been zero since tennis borrowed it, and a carl is Chaucer's peasant — old vocabulary standing in for a Spanish court.
explanation.definitionFit: pretender Don -> CARLOS: the Spanish claimant whose supporters, the Carlists, fought three wars for his branch of the royal line.

clue.text: Fate is pursuing learner with pains

indicators.note: One thing pursuing another follows along behind it, so those letters are added at the end of what has already been built.

parts.note: a learner driver carries L-plates
aches are dull pains
the clue's own verb, taken as two letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fate is pursuing' reads as one ominous phrase, which hides the fact that the 'is' has already stopped being grammar and become letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fate -> LACHESIS: one of the three Greek Fates, the sister who measures out the thread of a life, so the capital F names her by example.

clue.text: Blooming fellow needs taking down

parts.note: F is fellow, the letter in FRS after an academic's name
to take something down is to lower it

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two pieces and no indicator at all: the only trick is that 'blooming' is the definition and not the mild swear word.
explanation.definitionFit: Blooming -> FLOWERING: both mean in flower, and the surface leans on the other blooming, the one that means confounded.

clue.text: Rod collects wood and stone to make item of furniture

indicators.note: To collect things is to gather them in, so the rod closes around what it picks up instead of lying next to it.

parts.note: a wand is a slender rod
ash is a hardwood, a wood before it is a residue
ST is the abbreviation for the stone, fourteen pounds

explanation.walkthrough: Both materials are being used in their crossword senses rather than their obvious ones, which is what makes the builder's-yard surface hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: item of furniture -> WASHSTAND: the bedroom table that held the basin and jug before houses had plumbing, furniture named by its use.

clue.text: See 17
A useless beginning — what's after lasts, possibly

indicators.note: 'Possibly' says the words are not to be taken as they stand, which frees their letters to be set down in some other order.

parts.note: the ten letters of these two words, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is where the clue splits, and the (5,5) is the tell: the two words on the right have exactly ten letters between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A useless beginning -> FALSE START: a start ruled invalid and run again, so the beginning counted for nothing — the athletics sense.

clue.text: Beginning of intensive care organised to save old boy reliant on oxygen

indicators.note: Something organised has been put in an order somebody chose, so these letters are free to be set down in a different one.
To save a thing is to keep hold of it, and what is kept is kept within — the two letters are held inside the rest.
The beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, so the long word beside it gives up one letter only.

parts.note: the letter this word starts with
four more letters of fodder, taken as they stand
OB is an old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.walkthrough: 'Intensive care' and 'old boy' both read as hospital furniture; only one letter of the first survives, and the second is an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: reliant on oxygen -> AEROBIC: aerobic exercise and aerobic bacteria alike need air to work, aer- being the Greek for air.

clue.text: A coterie's unusual mysteries?

indicators.note: What is unusual is not in its usual arrangement, so these letters will not stay in the order the clue hands them over in.

parts.note: the nine letters of these words in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: A coterie is a small circle that keeps itself to itself, so the surface and the answer describe the same clique — only the letters move.
explanation.definitionFit: mysteries -> ESOTERICA: things kept for the initiated, arcana rather than puzzles, which is the older sense the plural noun carries.

clue.text: Cry in the country — gentry ultimately trapped in multi-storey house?

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes last of all, so the closing letter of the word before it is the one taken.

parts.note: a building of many storeys is tall

indicators.note: Something trapped in a place cannot get out of it, so the letter is held between the others rather than added on.

parts.note: the last letter of this word
HO is the abbreviation for house on an address

explanation.walkthrough: 'Multi-storey' promises a car park and delivers an adjective, and the question mark is there because the house is an abbreviation, not a home.
explanation.definitionFit: Cry in the country -> TALLY-HO: the huntsman's shout on sighting the fox, so 'the country' means the hunting field rather than a nation.

clue.text: Stylish dressmaking not in fashion — external remedy needed

indicators.note: An external remedy is applied on the outside, so the cure goes round the other letters instead of joining on to them.

parts.note: a remedy is a cure
what is no longer in fashion is out

explanation.walkthrough: The medical half of the clue is doing the wrapping, and 'not in fashion' sits in a clue about fashion without being about it at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish dressmaking -> COUTURE: the French word for the high-fashion trade, clothes cut to a designer's own patterns rather than bought off the peg.

clue.text: Trendy business not enjoying healthy state

parts.note: what is trendy is in
a firm is a business

explanation.walkthrough: IN for trendy is the crossword's other 'in' — fashionable rather than inside — and here it doubles as the prefix that reverses the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: not enjoying healthy state -> INFIRM: infirm means feeble or ailing, especially through age, so the phrase spells out the negative the prefix carries.

clue.text: Punished rogue primarily, one is in stir, right?

definitions.text: Punished rogue primarily, one is in stir, right?

indicators.note: Stir is what you do to a mixture, so the words caught in it come out with their letters in a different order.
What is primary comes first, so each of the two words before it gives up its opening letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the first letters of the two words
these five letters stirred into another order
R is right, as on a map or a stage direction

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: the sentence describes the man and builds him at the same time, with 'stir' meaning jail and mixture at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a rogue caught and locked up is serving his sentence, and stir has been slang for jail since the 1850s.

clue.text: See problem with drinking too much port? Switch off

parts.note: lo is the old imperative meaning see or behold

parts.words: problem with drinking too much port
parts.note: gout is the joint disease long blamed on port and rich living

explanation.walkthrough: Gout was the rich man's complaint, pinned for two centuries on fortified wine, which is why the port is doing all the work in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Switch off -> LOG OUT: ending your session on a machine you are signed in to, the everyday way of shutting a computer down for the night.

clue.text: Let me have a piece of string immediately

indicators.note: A piece of something is part of it and not the whole, so the answer is a run of letters cut out of the words that follow.

parts.note: the last letter of the first word joins the first four of the second

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers nearly always straddle a join between words, and this one takes a single letter from the first — the least you can take and still call it a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Let me have -> GIMME: 'gimme' is 'give me' as it is actually said, and in golf a gimme is the short putt an opponent concedes on that request.

clue.text: Leader of America having courageous style? Is twisted inside, showing bluntness

indicators.note: Something twisted has been turned right round, so those two letters are read the other way about.
The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so the country beside it contributes one letter only.

parts.note: the letter this word begins with

indicators.note: Inside says the piece belongs within the word rather than before or after it.

parts.note: to act in a courageous style is to act bravely
the clue's own word, turned back to front

explanation.walkthrough: 'Courageous style' means 'in a courageous manner', which is how a setter clues an adverb without ever using the word manner.
explanation.definitionFit: showing bluntness -> ABRASIVELY: an abrasive scours a surface, and someone who speaks abrasively rubs people the wrong way — bluntness that grates.

clue.text: Muck covering a woman lured into the garden?

indicators.note: Something covering another thing lies over it on both sides, so the muck wraps the letter instead of coming before it.

parts.note: muck is mud
the article, taken as a single letter

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters, three of them muck, and the whole clue turns on remembering one Victorian song lyric.
explanation.definitionFit: woman lured into the garden -> MAUD: Tennyson's 'Come into the garden, Maud' is the invitation, so the answer is named by the poem's most quoted line.

clue.text: Little woman grabbing baddy, head of English in school

indicators.note: To grab someone is to take hold and keep them, so whoever is grabbed ends up held inside the word.

parts.note: Amy March is one of Alcott's Little Women
a cad is the mild-mannered villain of older fiction

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter at the top of it, so the language beside it gives up one letter.

parts.note: E is the standard shortening of English

explanation.walkthrough: Both people are stock characters of the crossword rather than of the school story, which is exactly what makes them findable.
explanation.definitionFit: school -> ACADEMY: an academy is a school, usually one teaching a specialism — riding, military, dramatic art — or in England one outside council control.

clue.text: What Adam became after realisation of nudity? Fellow looking embarrassed

definitions.text: What Adam became after realisation of nudity

parts.note: a cove is an old slang fellow, Dickens's word rather than a bay
embarrassment shows as going red in the face

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns you the first half is a story rather than a synonym, and the second half is two pieces of plain slang.
explanation.definitionFit: What Adam became after realisation of nudity -> COVERED: Genesis has him sew fig leaves together the moment he notices, so covered is the plain result.
